— producing components for long- and medium-range strike UAVs, as well as assembling and storing boosters used in Flamingo cruise missiles;

— producing components for long- and medium-range strike UAVs, carrying out large-component assembly of fixed-wing UAVs, and storing UAVs;

Antonov State Enterprise
— producing the long-range An-196 “Lyutyi” UAV and developing and manufacturing various types of manned aircraft;

— storing M-900 thermobaric aerial bombs, anti-tank mines, and ammunition for Baba Yaga-type UAVs.

•
Martusivka Transport and Logistics Center (Zamler Group logistics center)
— storing and distributing dual-use goods, including those used in the production of long- and medium-range UAVs, robotic systems, and electronic warfare equipment;
•
Brovary fuel and lubricant warehouse
— storing up to 8,000 cubic meters of fuel intended for the Ukrainian Armed Forces.
In addition, on the evening of August 19, warehouses containing military equipment were hit at the ports of Chornomorsk and Pivdennyi.

In a rare occurrence, a Russian Su-35S multirole fighter crossed into Ukrainian airspace, flew over the town of Uhroidy in Sumy Oblast, and launched a Kh-59/69 cruise missile at Sumy City before safely returning to Kursk Oblast.
Normally, Su-35S, Su-30SM/SM2, and Su-34 aircraft launch glide bombs and other guided munitions from roughly 50 km behind the frontline to minimize the risk of interception by Ukrainian air defenses.
It may have been an attempt to test Ukraine’s air defense response, but apparently no interception followed. Russia may be increasingly confident that Ukraine currently lacks sufficient PAC-2/3 interceptor missiles to pose a significant threat to its aircraft.

Private Chinese space company LandSpace’s Zhuque-3 Y2 reusable launch vehicle successfully achieved orbital insertion and first-stage recovery.
